newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa firm, but fails to clear nearby hurdle.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa firm, but fails to clear nearby hurdle.

text.p: London cocoa futures pared gains on Tuesday, slipping below a technical hurdle after an earlier breakthrough.

The market's initial strength was dampened after a profit taking bout in New York. Some London traders said this was triggered by a 2,370-lot rise in open positions suggesting a further increase in longs.
"It tends to suggest that the market has now found brand new longs in New York yesterday. That was construed as being slightly bearish to the market," said one trader.
But a corollary of that view was that the remaining shorts and fresh buying could keep the market buoyant.

Credit Lyonnais Rouse was said to have offered 400 lots of May in London, sending the contract down to 1,030 stg a tonne after it had seen an intraday peak of 1,048 stg -- a new seven-month high. But it then recovered again.
"The market said 'thank you very much', took them in and off it ran again," said the trader.
Prudential Bache and Phibro were said to be buying, mainly on May.

At the close, May stood near the day's low at 1,033 stg, just three stg up from Monday. A robust 12,341 lots changed hands, including some 3,500 lots of against actuals across the board, traders said.
"The market is stuck. It feels a bit toppy and everyone wants to sell short but nobody has got the guts to do it," said the trader.
The change of direction in New York speculative positions was indicated in Friday's CFTC report by a large shift to longs.
But traders said the CFTC data also suggested that trade and industry were the best sellers to the funds on the way up, and they were now hoping for a retracement.
Structure trading was thin on Tuesday but May/July traded into 5-6, then out to 9-10 while Sept/Dec was at three value after five.
In other news, brokers GNI said Ivorian arrivals data was pointing at a crop of 1.1 million tonnes.
But the extent of a revision in the global deficit estimate, which GNI put at 180,000 tonnes in January, depended on first quarter grind figures, Lawrence Eagles, head of research said.
